title: 'It stood like a serpent right there staring at us': American who survived deadly Nepal flood tells her story - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
description: 'It stood like a serpent right there staring at us': American who survived deadly Nepal flood tells her story  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
publisher.title: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
full_article:
KATHMANDU, NEPAL -- Anjana Raja had long dreamed of traveling to Nepal as part of a spiritual journey to Mount Kailash ever since she was a teenager, she said.

When she and her husband finally got to make that dream a reality this month, the California mom of two told ABC News she could not have imagined that trip would force them into survival mode as they found themselves nearly swept up in the deadly landslide flood that hit the region Wednesday.

Nepal survivor Anjana Raja speaks to ABC News. ABC News

Raja recalled sitting on a bus with her husband traveling to the Chinese border on Wednesday when, all of a sudden, the driver and front passengers fled the bus and she saw the landslide coming toward their vehicle.

Related Hundreds dead as over 2,000 remain missing in massive Nepal-Tibet flood

"It was water mixed with the mud that was a good 50 to 60 feet high. It stood like a serpent right there staring at us," Raja told ABC News. "Like a cobra's head staring at you."

Firefighters conduct a search and rescue operation at a damaged road leading to Gyirong Port after a mudslide, in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China, August 28, 2026. Cnsphoto via Reuters

Raja said she didn't hesitate and grabbed her sling bag and turned to her husband, Pattabiraman Venkatesan.

"I grabbed him by the collar, and I said, 'Run, we need to go right now,'" she said.

"I didn't even give time to act. I just said, 'Leave the bus right away or we're gonna die,'" Raja added.

A collapsed bridge and damaged settlements debris and mud covers an area following flash floods, August 28, 2026 in DeviGhat village, Nepal. Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images

As of Friday, as intense search and rescue efforts continue, 584 people have been reported dead in the floods, according to the Nepal National Disaster Management Authority and Chinese government.

Meanwhile, over 2,400 people were reported missing according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and the Chinese government.

Faced with the huge wall of water and mud, the couple and other bus passengers ran to a camp right next to the bus and made their way to higher ground as the water hit and completely flooded the streets, she said.

"We just blindly...climbed. We didn't even know what direction ... There was no guide for us, there was nobody, we were just frantically running. Running, literally running. It was slushy, it was muddy, we were climbing rocks, which was slippery. We just ran for our life," she said.

Popular Reads 'Inexplicable' order probed as cause of train crash that killed at least 69: Official Oct 29 Inside the hunt for killer of University of North Carolina student found beaten 2 days ago 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Oct 29

"When we reached the second level ... I saw the water come up to the slope and move our bus. I told my husband 'That's it, we're gone. We're going to die,'" she said.

They ultimately made their way up to the third level of the camp and they watched in shock as the wall of water rushed past them.

From their point they could see vehicles, objects and even people be taken in by the water's power, although the water never reached their level.

"It just came like a roar, it sucked a bunch of buses, SUVs, people, the basecamp, everything -- took it in, turned it, turned it all upside down and dumped it into the ground," Raja said.

Residents salvage belongings from their destroyed home following flash floods, August 28, 2026 in Devighat, Nepal. Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

Eventually, Raja said she and her husband were able to contact her daughter Amanda, a physician, back in California and they have been in constant contact. The couple also has a college-age son.

Related What caused Nepal flood? Scientist says it was enormous landslide, glacier fall

Raja commended the actions of first responders, especially how they worked to take care of the most vulnerable victims.

"What I really loved is his focus was not foreign nationals, nor U.S. citizens. He looked at us as humans," she said of her rescuer.

Raja said that the entire experience has left a long-lasting impression on her.

"I know time will heal but I think, with all this what happened, I think I've become stronger mentally, emotionally. I'm not crying so that's a good thing," she said.

Nepal survivor Anjana Raja speaks to ABC News. ABC News

Still, Raja said she and her husband are determined to return and complete their journey to Mount Kailash.

"I am determined to," she said.

full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 1: Travel content creators from seven countries have arrived in Nepal. The Nepal Tourism Board (NTB) collaborated with TikTok to bring them to Nepal.

The initiative aims to promote Nepal's touristic destinations globally via international social media including digital platforms. The travel content creators hailing from France, Portugal, Tunisia, South Korea, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Bangladesh and Sri Lanka have been invited to Nepal.

During their stay in Nepal, the travelers will produce videos and digital contents capturing Nepal’s natural beauty, cultural heritage, adventure activities and various other facets of tourism. Such content will be shared with a global audience via social media platforms, including TikTok.

NTB senior manager Surya Thapaliya said three creators from the UAE and Tunisia are busy in exploring Pokhara, while others are travelling across Kathmandu.

Their creations are to highlight tourist destinations such as Pokhara, Chitwan and Bardiya as well as other sites of cultural, historical and tourism significance across Nepal. They are expected to showcase Nepal’s Himalayan beauty, cultural heritage, adventure tourism and local lifestyle to the global community, it is said. (RSS)

title: Nepal court gives 3 months for cannabis cultivation rules — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal court gives 3 months for cannabis cultivation rules — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal’s Supreme Court has ordered the government to introduce, within three months, a regulatory framework for the controlled commercial cultivation and production of cannabis for medical, scientific, agricultural, horticultural and industrial purposes. This was reported by Kathmandu Post.

Licensing and oversight

The court ordered the authorities to develop rules, standards and procedures to implement the Narcotic Drugs Control Act of 1976. The new provisions must regulate the licensing of cannabis cultivation, production, processing, storage, use, sale, distribution, import and export for the specified purposes.

The decision was issued on May 18, 2025, by a panel of judges Nahakul Subedi and Til Prasad Shrestha following a petition filed by lawyer Saroj Adhikari and other petitioners. The full text of the verdict was published recently.

The court noted that the government had long failed to use its authority to develop the rules required for the practical implementation of the law. In the court’s view, this hindered the regulation of cannabis cultivation and use.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Recreational use separately

The Supreme Court stressed that the mechanism must provide for strict oversight: allowing licensed cultivation and production while preventing illegal cultivation, production, manufacturing and distribution.

The rules must comply with national legislation and the 1961 UN Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, including its provisions on the control and supervision of cannabis cultivation.

Regarding recreational cannabis use, the court noted that current legislation does not explicitly provide for it. The court drew the attention of the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers to the need for broader consultations with experts and stakeholders before possible amendments to the law, taking into account Nepal’s social, economic and cultural context.

title: Nepal, Bhutan seek dedicated Himalayan climate agenda at COP31 - www.carboncopy.info
description: Nepal, Bhutan seek dedicated Himalayan climate agenda at COP31  www.carboncopy.info
publisher.title: www.carboncopy.info
full_article:
Nepal and Bhutan have jointly proposed a dedicated agenda item on rising temperatures in mountain regions at the COP31 climate summit, seeking greater international attention to the risks facing the Himalayas and communities dependent on its ecosystems.

The two countries have asked the United Nations climate conference to include an item titled “1.5°C Warming in Mountains” in its supplementary provisional agenda. Nepal's Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment, Geeta Chaudhary, submitted the proposal on behalf of both governments under Rule 12 of the conference's draft rules of procedure.

The proposal comes amid growing concern over climate-related disasters in the Himalayan region, including floods in Nepal's Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems in August and a glacial lake outburst flood in Bhutan in October.



Also Read: Nepal’s Floods Put Climate Finance Shortfall in Focus Ahead of COP31

The submission warns that rising temperatures are accelerating changes in glaciers, snow cover and permafrost, threatening water supplies, biodiversity, food production, energy systems and the livelihoods of mountain communities.

It also highlights the consequences for populations downstream. Rivers originating in mountain regions provide freshwater to more than two billion people across Asia and beyond, making changes in the Himalayas a concern for water, food and energy security across the region.

COP31 will be held in Antalya, Türkiye, from Nov. 9 to 20. The proposal's submission does not mean the agenda item has been adopted, with its inclusion subject to the conference's formal procedures.

Nepal and Bhutan have proposed four areas for international action. These include more research into how 1.5°C warming and temperature overshoot could affect mountain regions, an annual high-level dialogue on mountain climate issues, a UN climate programme focused on mountain ecosystems, and greater recognition of mountain-specific needs in climate adaptation, finance and loss and damage arrangements.



Also Read: As Nepal rebuilds, a climate-vulnerable nation tests the world’s response

The proposal argues that mountain ecosystems need greater recognition in global climate negotiations because of their importance to both ecological stability and human welfare.

It cites the damage caused by the August 2026 Bhotekoshi disaster in Nepal, estimating losses at about $2.7 billion and reconstruction needs at $4.7 billion, equivalent to roughly 10% of the country's gross domestic product.





Caption: Important figures to look out for Nepal's disaster (Visuals by Arkatapa Basu)

The two countries say stronger cross-border cooperation, disaster preparedness, early warning systems and access to climate finance are needed to address risks that extend beyond national boundaries.



Caption: Figures for climate finance goal, fund for responding to loss and damage (Visuals by Arkatapa Basu)

The submission draws on provisions of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change that recognise the specific needs of countries with fragile ecosystems, including mountain regions.

Nepali security forces are trying to rescue six Indian tourists who have been stranded by heavy snowfall in the Himalayas near Nepal's deepest lake since Saturday afternoon.

The group, four men and two women, is stuck at Danigad in Shey-Phoksundo National Park, in Dolpa district in the remote north-west of Nepal, according to the district administration.

The Shey Phoksundo lake in the rural municipality of the same name is Nepal's deepest lake at an altitude of 3,600metres (11,800ft) and with the estimated depth of 145m (475ft).
